title: Content in the System
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Content in the System.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content standards belong in a design system because reusable components carry meaning as well as visual form. Define labels, voice, error structures, confirmation patterns, empty states, variable content rules, and localisation constraints. This makes clear language easier to apply consistently.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content design must remain contextual. A system can give principles and patterns, but it should not turn every message into a generic template. The component should expose the information a writer needs to express the real consequence and next action.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Content is part of the behavioural contract
turns.text: What changes when we look at content is part of the behavioural contract?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: System content has three layers. Voice principles establish durable qualities such as direct, respectful, and calm. Content patterns describe how meaning changes across recurring situations—errors, confirmation, empty states, permission requests, progress, and destructive actions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Component content rules specify the slots, constraints, and relationships required for one implementation. A slogan about tone cannot replace any of these layers.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The content API encodes meaning rather than accepting arbitrary strings. A referral-status component receives a governed state, timestamp source, responsible actor, next-action type, and optional explanation. The rendering layer selects tested language and exposes controlled extension points for legitimate clinical detail.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This reduces accidental contradiction across UI, email, SMS, and support. It also makes localisation and accessibility review possible before a product team invents a sentence under deadline pressure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: payment failure?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Something went wrong” is visually reusable and operationally useless. A payment pattern needs to distinguish bank decline, expired method, network uncertainty, duplicate-risk state, and merchant rejection because each permits a different next action. The system should prevent a team from confidently saying “not charged” when the transaction state is unknown.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content governance protects truth under uncertainty.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at treat language as system behaviour?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define content principles, voice, terminology, grammar, action labels, error patterns, status, confirmation, and accessibility guidance alongside visual components. A button API without rules for naming the action still creates inconsistent decisions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design content slots around purpose and limits. Specify required labels, helper text, error association, dynamic values, localisation expansion, pluralisation, and screen-reader context. Avoid placeholder strings that make layouts look stable while real languages and data break them.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Govern shared terminology through a controlled vocabulary and ownership. When product domains need different words, document the audience and meaning rather than forcing superficial consistency. Test component content in the complete task: the same phrase can be clear in one state and ambiguous in another.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at systematise meaning without flattening context?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The system documents terminology, definitions, prohibited ambiguity, voice principles, localisation notes, and content accessibility. Content tokens are used carefully; a reusable string is appropriate only when meaning and grammar stay stable. Concatenating fragments can break translation and screen-reader comprehension.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Examples include realistic edge cases rather than polished success copy.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content governance needs ownership and contribution paths. Otherwise teams fork labels and messages as quickly as they fork visual components.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Content patterns should define the information a component needs, not only a string length. A confirmation may need action, object, status, time, consequence, and next step; an error may need problem, location, repair, and support route.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Document voice principles, label grammar, punctuation, capitalisation, variable rules, truncation, translation, and accessible names so content is treated as behaviour rather than decoration.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Create components with meaningful slots and constraints. “Title” and “body” may be too generic when a message needs an outcome or next action. Work with writers and localisation specialists early; a concise English label may become much longer or grammatically different elsewhere.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Allow contextual authoring where meaning changes, while ensuring the base pattern prevents known ambiguity and inaccessible defaults.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Lorem-ipsum system: components are designed without realistic content or states. Template voice: reusable wording erases the actual consequence or task. Truncation as solution: important information is clipped rather than structurally supported. Unowned copy: no one maintains terminology, examples, or translation guidance.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: One confirmation says “Done,” another says “Success,” and a third says “Your request is being processed.” The words are not decoration; they change whether people understand the state.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Worked example For a destructive action, the system defines title, consequence, primary action named with the real verb, cancel path, and recovery information. Products supply the object and irreversible effect; they cannot replace it with “Continue.” Translation tests reveal whether the component accommodates longer action labels.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Screen-reader review checks that context is not carried only by the surrounding visual layout. Content rules have become executable quality rather than a page in a style guide. Components make interaction repeatable; content makes that interaction understandable. lesson 52 begins the practical work of introducing a system through a focused pilot.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Compare confirmation labels across a product. Are they systematically clear about outcome, state, and next action?
